words.definition: A person who works in politics, especially as an elected official.

words.definition: A formal process in which people vote to choose someone for a position.

words.definition: To formally choose someone or something, usually in an election.

words.definition: An organized effort to achieve a goal, especially winning an election.

words.definition: A plan of action agreed on by a government or organization.

words.definition: A system of government in which people vote for their leaders.

words.definition: A legally recognized member of a country.

words.definition: The group of elected people who make laws in some countries.

words.definition: To act or speak officially on behalf of someone or a group.
words.example: Each member of parliament represents a local area.

words.definition: A formal discussion in which people express different opinions.

words.definition: A change made to improve a system, organization, or law.

words.definition: The power to give orders, make decisions, or enforce rules.

words.definition: Dishonest or illegal behavior, especially by people in positions of power.

words.definition: To publicly show strong disagreement with something.

words.definition: A person who controls, guides, or is in charge of a group or country.

words.definition: The political party or group that opposes the government in power.
words.example: The opposition criticized the new policy.

text: In a democracy, citizens have the right to vote for the people who will represent them in government. Every few years, an election is held, and different candidates present their policy ideas during a public campaign. Some candidates focus on reform, promising to improve healthcare, education, or the economy, while others prefer to keep things as they are. Once elected, politicians usually work in parliament, where laws are debated and, if enough members agree, eventually passed. Although the government has the authority to make important decisions, an opposition party exists to question its choices and offer alternative solutions. This system, in theory, helps prevent corruption and protects the rights of ordinary citizens. However, if people lose trust in their leaders, they may protest in the streets to demand change. Money is another important issue in politics because governments need tax revenue to pay for schools, hospitals, and roads. As a result, debates about how much tax citizens should pay are often at the center of every election. Understanding these basic ideas helps people become more active and informed members of society.
